The single-pass tune of Qwen2.5 Coder 1.5B finished without errors. It took 7,107 item answers in all and saved the profile to `~/.modelduck/profiles/qwen2.5-coder-1.5b-instruct-q4.json`.

**Device and load settings:**
- **Backend:** your RX 9060 XT (Vulkan, all layers) produced 122.5 tokens/s against 16.75 on the CPU, about 7× faster, with all 6 test answers correct.
- **Context and memory:** 16,384-token context, full-precision (f16) KV cache, batch size 512, 12 threads. Flash attention and mmap stayed on auto.
- **Speed presets:** Fastest uses 12 threads and Light uses 8. Otherwise they are the same.

**Per-task presets:**

| Task | Score [95% range] | vs defaults | Temp | Repeat penalty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chat | 83.3% [64–93] | +2.7 pts | 0 | 1.1 |
| Code | 87.5% [69–96] | +6.9 pts | 0.2 | 1.0 |
| Math | 71.4% [50–86] | +12.7 pts | 0.2 | 1.0 |
| Long context | 90.9% [62–98] | +3.0 pts | 0 | 1.1 |

All four tasks share: maxTokens 512, minP 0.05, topP 0.9, topK 40, reasoning off, promptRepeat 1.

**What stands out:**
- **None of the 21 "thinking" one-sentence prompts beat the default system prompt** ("You are a precise assistant. Follow the requested output format exactly…") on any task. On long-context recall, all 21 tied with it at 90.9%. For a 1.5B model, a format instruction helps more than a style one.
- **Reasoning on and promptRepeat 2 never helped.** promptRepeat 2 even cost a recall item and made answers about 60% slower.
- **The gains over defaults are not proven yet.** They point the right way, but none is statistically significant: Math's +12.7 points has p=0.375, and the others p=1. A single pass with up to 24 items per task can't separate small differences. More items or more passes would be needed to make them conclusive.
- **This profile was measured on the old test suite (v8).** The app will show a "test suite changed" warning on it and still use it. Clicking **Re-tune ⚠** in the Bench table re-measures it on v9, which adds the new long coding and long bug-fix questions.

### ADR-034: A tune can run only chosen settings
- **Date**: 2026-10-31
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: Whole stages could already be chosen (`--stages`), but the user wants to run a single section, for example only the context size, or only the quality and speed settings, without redoing anything else.
- **Decision**: `--settings <names>` (API and scheduler: `settings`) runs only those settings, in stage order, each re-measured even if tuned before, on top of every other setting's current best. Valid names are listed by `settingNames()` (device, contextSize, kvCache, flashAttention, useMmap, batchSize, threads, checkpointing, temperature, maxTokens, repeatPenalty, minP, topP, topK, systemPrompt, reasoning, promptRepeat); unknown names are refused. Only settings measured now or before are stored, never untouched defaults. A partial selection never marks a stage finished; a stage finished before stays finished and its statistics are refreshed only when the stage is complete. An explicit selection always runs (no skip), still refused on a stale profile without `--force`.
- **Consequences**: Re-tuning one setting takes minutes. Light keeps its earlier thread count unless threads were re-measured. A real run re-tuning only the context size of a SmolLM2 profile swept four sizes, stored only `contextSize` and left every other stage untouched.

### ADR-035: Suite v9 adds 44 of our own coding and bug-fix questions, long ones included
- **Date**: 2026-10-31
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: The user asked for many more of ModelDuck's own coding and bug-fix questions, including long coding tasks and long bug fixes. The code task tuned on 24 own items, all short, with 256-token budgets.

- **Date**: 2026-10-31
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: The engine created each `LlamaChatSession` with the system prompt, then called `setChatHistory(history)` with the earlier turns. node-llama-cpp's `setChatHistory` replaces the whole history, including the system message the constructor put first, so no system prompt ever reached the model: chat, the benchmark and every tune answered under the model template's own default. content.text:
ModelDuck is published: it's in the private repo **https://github.com/AegeanWorks/Modelduck**, and GitHub's `master` is at commit `9d3b185`, the same as local.

**What it took:**
- **The 21 directive prompts:** they're the prompt stage's default now; the thinking prompts can still be used from a saved grid.
- **Secret scan:** it flagged 8 lines that are ordinary code, not credentials (a KV-cache size calculation, a model name, a couple of cache keys). Each now carries the repo's `aikit:allow-secret` marker.
- **Squash, as you chose:** GitHub has one commit holding the full current project. The old commit history is on a local branch, `history-backup`, which is not pushed.

**A big bug fixed along the way.** I found it when your prompt-only run on Qwen2.5 Coder scored all 22 system prompts exactly the same.
- **The bug:** the engine discarded the system prompt every time it set up a chat, so no system prompt ever reached the model. That covered normal chats, the benchmark and every tune; the model just used its built-in default.
- **The fix:** a test that failed before the change and passes after it. On the real Coder model, a pirate system prompt now changes the answer to "Two plus two equals four. Arr!".
- **What it invalidates:**
  - Both "no prompt beat the default" results, so the comparison between your thinking prompts and the directives is still open.
  - Any setting tuned before the fix, including the Coder profile's sampling settings, was measured without a system prompt.
  - The prompt-only run itself also stopped early, after the chat and code tasks, without running math or recall.

**Worth fixing:**
- **The GitHub repo description is wrong.** It says "No GPU", but ModelDuck now runs on your GPU through Vulkan. It came from the project's saved description; I can correct it if you want.
- **Your Coder profile needs a re-tune.** Run it from the Bench table with Re-tune ⚠, or just its prompt settings, to get real system-prompt results now that the fix is in.

On your earlier agent question: nothing needed changing. **explorer**, your only search agent, already runs on haiku, the cheapest model.

I made the fixes, added items to all the thin tasks plus multi-file codebase tests for the coder, and pushed everything to GitHub (`14aaf2b`). All 303 tests and the delivery checks pass.

**Fixes:**
- **GitHub description:** the "No GPU" claim is gone. It now reads "Runs on the CPU or a Vulkan GPU", both on GitHub and in the README.
- **The prompt-only run that stopped after the code task:** the log showed no error. It died during the memory stall (about 1.2 GB of RAM free), so it looks like the machine, not ModelDuck. I'll watch for it on the next real run.

**More items, for real statistics:**

| Task | Items before | Items now | Items scored in the final step |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chat | 54 | 54 | 24 → 48 |
| Code | 88 | 100 | 24 → 48 |
| Math | 21 | 51 | 21 → 48 |
| Long context | 11 | 51 | 11 → 48 |

- **Math:** 30 new word problems (rates, percentages, ages, time, averages). Each answer is worked out a second time in the tests.
- **Long context:** 40 new items generated from a fixed seed, so they're the same on every run. They cover PIN lookups at different depths in registers of 20, 50 and 80 rows, reverse lookups, the latest status in a delivery log, the sum of two balances, and counting.
- With 48 paired items instead of 11–24, real differences of roughly 15 points or more should now show up as significant.
- **Cost:** a tune takes roughly twice as long per stage.

**Codebase tests for the coder:** 12 new items built on three small multi-file projects (a shop with tax, a search index, a meeting calendar). Each project includes an unrelated file the model has to ignore. The questions are:
- **6 × write a new function** that uses the project's existing helpers;
- **3 × fix a bug from a user's report;**
- **3 × name the function** that contains a reported bug.

When scored, the rest of the project is loaded alongside the model's answer, so the answer only passes if it actually fits the codebase. The tests check that every reference answer passes and every shipped bug really fails.

**Two things to know:**
- **Every saved profile now shows a "test suite changed" warning,** because the suite moved to v10. They all need a re-tune anyway: the system-prompt fix means everything tuned before it was measured without a system prompt.
- **12 codebase items is a start, not a strong signal yet.** If you want, I can add more codebases, for example larger projects with 6–10 files, or tasks that change two files at once.

`GET /api/benchmarks` returns the two baseline phases, recent linked runs, own
versus public item rates and recommendations from the latest model run. The run
endpoints are loopback-only and start one child benchmark at a time; they refuse
while a reply is generating so the CPU measurements stay comparable.
`POST /api/benchmarks/base` saves one model-phase variant as the base the next
chat-phase run loads. `POST /api/benchmarks/run` with `{"phase":"tune","model":"<id>"}`
tunes one installed model (optional `tasks` and `force`); a saved profile is reused
unless `force` is true, and `stages` (device, quality, speed, sampling, prompt) runs only some of them; the
profile is saved after every finished setting, so a stopped tune is applied as far as it got and resumes later.
`POST /api/tune/start` with `{"models":"all"}` (or a list of model ids) tunes several models
side by side: device probes first, then 1 CPU lane and 2 GPU lanes by default (`lanes` in
`tune-grid.json`, set per PC); speed measurements pause the other tunes so they stay clean. `GET /api/profiles/:id` returns the profile with `stale` and
plain-language `warnings` when the test suite, test items, runtime, CPU or model file
changed since it was measured; a stale profile is still used until it is re-tuned.

The host's loopback UI stays key-free. Authentication covers the OpenAI-compatible
API and, when the request comes from another machine, the UI/API routes as well.
When enabled, send `Authorization: Bearer <key>` or `X-API-Key: <key>`; keys are
shown once and only their SHA-256 hashes are stored. A LAN browser is prompted
for the key once and keeps it in session storage.

input.command:
cat >> .aikit/decisions.md <<'EOF'

### ADR-040: Part runs re-measure chosen parts on top of the saved rest
- **Date**: 2026-10-31
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: The user wants to run one part of the tune for every model: only the CPU-versus-GPU probe, one setting, or only the prompt stage. Choosing a stage that was already done skipped it, and Run all started every stale profile over, so a prompt-only run after a suite change discarded each model's device, load and sampling results and measured prompts on defaults.
- **Decision**: A part run (some stages, or some settings, for one model or for all) measures the chosen parts again on top of the saved rest, even when they are done or the profile is stale; a partial stage resumes instead of starting over. `planTune` returns the parts it re-runs (`rerun`) and removes their progress so they start fresh; `isPartRun` is shared with the server, whose `forceStale` now starts stale profiles over only for a whole tune. A profile may carry `measuredUnder`, the fingerprint each part was measured under when they differ; `loadProfile` reports staleness across all of them, lists the old parts in `staleParts` and adds a warning naming them. This lifts ADR-034's refusal of an explicit selection on a stale profile; the test "an explicit selection of settings always runs" now expects the part run to proceed.
- **Consequences**: A device-only run of a stale Qwen2.5 Coder profile re-measured the probe under suite v11 and kept every other result, recorded as measured under the older suite. A full re-tune still needs `force` (Re-tune ⚠) on a stale profile.
EOF

content.text:
Everything you asked for is in and pushed to GitHub. All 311 tests pass, and each change was checked in the real app or with a real tune run.

**Running parts of the tune, for one model or all of them**
- Picking only some stages (for example just Device, the CPU-vs-GPU probe, or just Prompt) or only some settings now measures just those again. Everything else the model already has is kept.
- Before, an already-finished stage was skipped. Worse, on an out-of-date profile (which is every profile right now, after the test-suite update) Run all wiped the profile and measured the chosen part on default settings.
- Each profile now records which test-suite version each part was measured under, so the app warns about only the parts that are out of date.
- Real check: a device-only run on the Coder profile re-measured the probe (GPU 117.6 tokens/s vs CPU 22.1) and kept every other result.
- The model row's Re-tune button had the same wipe problem. It now starts over only for a whole tune.

**Reasoning in the tune is now off vs fully on.** It used to compare off with "auto", which only adds a short nudge. "On" is now the "think before answering" setting.

**More codebase tests for the coder.** Three larger projects (a bank ledger, an order-and-shipping service, a Markdown renderer) of six or seven files each, with 12 new questions: write a function using the existing code, fix a reported bug, or name the function that has the bug. That makes 24 codebase questions in total.

**The Bench section.** I went through every screen of it myself.

| Problem I found | What it does now |
|---|---|
| About nine screens of scrolling | About 1½ screens by default |
| Reports and recommendations from old test suites (v4, v7, v8) open by default | Folded under the tuner, older suites shown only when you tick a box |
| Each report had a ~100-row item table | Folded into "Every item (N)" |
| Stages and settings had no explanations | Each stage says what it measures; settings are grouped by stage, with plain names and hover help |
| Every model said "Re-tune ⚠" without saying why | Each says why, e.g. "The test suite changed (v8 → v11)" |
| No way to see a model's results | A **Details** button shows each task's score, 95% range, change vs defaults and the chosen settings |
| Statistic tiles overlapped each other | They no longer overlap |

**What you need to know**
- **Someone else is editing ModelDuck's brand media in parallel.** `assets/social-preview.svg` and `.aikit/media.json` are being edited, and an AIKit media tool added `assets/screenshots/2026-10-31-home.png`, a copy of the welcome screenshot. The review entry is signed "human:owner", so I assume that's you or another session of yours. I didn't commit any of it.
- **I briefly moved those files aside** whenever a check or the push needed a clean folder. Each time I put them back only if nobody had written them in the meantime. All three are back as you left them and still uncommitted.
- **One process slip:** a UI commit went in before its UI check had passed. I undid it before anything was pushed, redid it properly, and now check the result in the same command.
- **To use all this:** every model needs a re-tune on the new test suite. A whole re-tune would also replace the old prompt and sampling results, which were measured while the system prompt was being dropped. Re-running only the parts you care about (for example the Prompt stage for all models) now keeps everything else.
Continue improving tuning ui and tuning mechanicsm

I'll take this in two parts:

- **The tuner's decision rule:** looking at whether it can tell a real improvement from noise.
- **The UI:** showing what each tune actually tried, not just what it picked.

Starting with how a winner is chosen:

### ADR-042: A setting changes only on a significant gain, and a tune that cannot load stops
- **Date**: 2026-10-31
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: On an axis's last rung the highest rate won and the current setting only won exact ties, so a challenger one lucky item ahead replaced it. With 22 system prompts scored at once, the best of many noisy rates is optimistic (the winner's curse), and earlier tunes moved settings on gains with p from 0.375 to 1. Separately, a real run with a broken Vulkan binary failed every answer, yet the tuner chose a prompt among 22 failures and saved 0% over the task's preset.
- **Decision**: A challenger that wins on quality alone replaces the current setting only when it beats it in the paired McNemar test (more items it alone gets right than items only the current one gets right) at `changeAlpha` (0.2) divided by the number of challengers; otherwise the current setting stays and the sweep records `kept`, naming the best challenger, both rates, p and the bar. Speed and memory ties keep their own rules. When every candidate of a rung fails, the current setting included, `Measurements.stop` ends every further measurement, the result carries `stopped`, and `runTune` refuses to save and reports why with a fix. The tuner's mechanics tests run with `changeAlpha: Infinity` (the rule off), since they check selection on 4-8 items; the rule and the stop have their own tests.
- **Consequences**: Tuned settings move less often and only on evidence, so presets stay at the suite defaults unless a change is real. A real run with the GPU broken stopped after 11 s with the reason and left the profile byte-identical.
EOF

content.text:
Your stage buttons are in, along with two fixes to how the tuner decides and one new view. Everything is tested (314 tests pass), checked in the real app or with real tune runs, and pushed to GitHub.

**Your request: a button for each stage**
- In each model's row, the stage chips (Device ✓, Quality, Speed, Sampling, Prompt) are now buttons.
- Clicking one runs just that stage for that model, even if it's already ✓, and ignores the checkboxes above.
- The result is saved and all other stages keep theirs. Every later tuning stage starts from the saved results, so if you re-run Device and it picks CPU, the following stages run on CPU.
- While a tune runs, the buttons are disabled and the stage in progress is highlighted.
- I clicked them in the real app: each sends exactly that one stage for that one model, and never the "from scratch" option.

**Tuning: settings now change only on real evidence**
- **The old rule:** a setting changed whenever another value scored even one item higher. That one item is usually luck, especially with 22 system prompts compared at once.
- **The new rule:** a setting changes only if the new value wins a paired statistical test against the current one. The bar is stricter the more values are compared, so 21 rival prompts need much stronger evidence than an on/off switch.
- When the current value stays, the tune records why: the best rival, both scores and the p-value.
- Your Coder profile shows why this matters. It has "Temperature: changed from 0.7 to 0 (p=1)", meaning no evidence at all.

**Tuning: a broken GPU can no longer damage results**
- This happened for real today. node-llama-cpp's Vulkan GPU check started failing while your graphics card reported OK.
- A test tune then failed every answer, still "picked" a prompt among the failures, and saved 0% over the recall preset. That was in a scratch copy, not your real profile.
- Now, if nothing can load, the tune stops and saves nothing new. Rerunning the same case stopped after 11 seconds with an explanation and left the profile unchanged.
- **The GPU fault itself is still there. Restarting the PC usually clears it,** and until then GPU tunes will stop at once with that message.

**New in the Bench section: "What was tried"**
- Under each model's Details, every setting now lists the values tried and their scores, which one won, and whether it changed or why it stayed.
- Changes from older tunes that weren't statistically meaningful are marked "Not significant: today's tuner would have kept 0.7".

**Process slip:** one commit went in while the README-length check was failing, because my command didn't stop on the failed check. I undid it before pushing, fixed the README and recommitted. Every commit command now stops when the check fails.

**Worth knowing:**
- **Your parallel media work is untouched.** The social-preview image, `media.json` and the new screenshot folder are still uncommitted, exactly as you left them.
- **Re-running Device on its own can leave later stages on the old device.** If the device changes, Quality, Speed and the rest still hold results measured on the previous one until you re-run them. I could have the app flag that automatically if you'd like.
Commit those graphical changes.
Before committing, I'll check the current state of those files, since they may have changed again since I last looked:

One more note: the project checks failed once in the middle of this, then passed on an immediate rerun with nothing changed. That points to an occasionally flaky timing-sensitive test, which I can track down if you want.
Think ways to improve tuning

Here are the improvements I'd make, most valuable first. Each comes from something we actually saw in today's runs.

**1. Confirm each preset on questions the tune never saw.** Today the preset is chosen and scored on the same questions, so the reported gain ("+12.7 pts vs defaults") is optimistic. That's the winner's curse again, at the preset level. Keep about a quarter of each task's questions aside, then compare the final preset with the defaults only on those. The UI would show that held-out gain as the honest number, and a preset that doesn't beat the defaults on unseen questions falls back to them.

**2. Stop comparing early once the answer is clear.** Every candidate currently answers a fixed 12, then 24, then 48 questions. A sequential test could drop a clearly worse value after about 12 questions and keep adding questions only when two values are close. The same time buys more statistical power exactly where it's needed. This matters most for the 22 system prompts, which are fully scored and are the most expensive stage.

**3. Tune settings that interact together.** The tuner adjusts one setting at a time, which misses pairs that only work together:
- **Reasoning on × answer length:** "think first" needs room. With the length capped at 512 tokens, reasoning on gets cut off and loses unfairly, so its budget should be raised when it's tried.
- **Temperature × answer length**, and **context size × KV-cache type** for memory.

Trying a few combinations of each known pair (not every combination of everything) would fix it.

**4. Choose the context size from real long inputs.** The longest test question is only about 1,300 tokens, so every context size from 2,048 to 16,384 scores the same. The Coder ended up with 16,384, which costs memory without any measured benefit. Either add a few genuinely long recall questions (8k and 16k tokens) so the choice reflects them, or treat context size as a memory budget ("largest that fits in free RAM/VRAM") rather than a quality setting.

**5. Make the stage dependencies explicit.** If a Device re-run moves a model from GPU to CPU, the Quality, Speed and later results were measured on the GPU. The app should mark those parts "measured on another device" (the same way it marks an older test suite), and the Device button could offer to re-run what depends on it. Also, check that the GPU actually starts *before* a tune begins, so a broken driver fails in one second rather than after the first full round.

**6. Start from a related model's results.** Qwen 0.5B Q4, Q5 and Q8 are the same model at different precisions. Instead of tuning each from scratch, start from a tuned sibling's settings and only confirm or adjust them. That should save hours per model.

**7. Show a real time estimate.** The current "≈ 9.3 h (upper bound)" assumes 3 s per answer, which is far off on your GPU (often around 0.2 s). Use the measured time per answer and the questions still left to show, per model, "about 25 min left".

**8. Spot-check saved presets now and then.** After a driver, runtime or test-suite change, re-measure each saved preset on about 12 questions. Only re-tune if it got clearly worse, instead of re-tuning everything just because the version changed.

**9. Two loose ends:**
- **The `tune:gate` baseline still doesn't exist,** so nothing catches a tuning regression.
- **One timing-sensitive test fails occasionally,** as it did once today.

### ADR-043: Context size is a memory budget, not a quality setting
- **Date**: 2026-10-31
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: The longest test question is about 1,300 tokens, so every context size from 2,048 to 16,384 answered the same, and the choice among them was noise; Qwen2.5 Coder ended up at 16,384, costing memory with no measured benefit. Longer questions (8k-16k tokens) would make every long-context answer slow on a CPU and still only push the choice to whatever the longest question needs.
- **Decision**: The `contextSize` axis is a budget step. `budgetContext` picks the largest listed size whose estimated load (weights, KV cache at the chosen type, runtime reserve) fits within 60% of the free memory of the chosen device (VRAM on a GPU, RAM on the CPU, the loaded model's own share counted as free; `LlamaEngine.availableMemory`), capped at the model's trained context; with nothing fitting, or memory or the KV shape unknown, it uses the smallest size and says so. No question is asked at any other size; the KV cache is still measured at the budgeted size, and the descent's second pass recomputes the budget for the chosen KV cache. The sweep records the reason. Without a budget hook (tests, the gate) the axis is measured as before. Separately, the timing-lock test "without a timing stage, a tune never pauses" now allows 1 s instead of 50 ms: only a pause could take long there, and 50 ms failed now and then on a loaded Windows disk.
- **Consequences**: A real context-only run of SmolLM2 on the CPU chose 8,192 because it was the largest that fit comfortably in the 1.1 GiB of free RAM. Profiles keep their earlier context until the context size is run again.
EOF

### ADR-044: Parts remember their device, and a tune checks the GPU before it starts
- **Date**: 2026-10-31
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: A stage button can re-run the device probe alone (ADR-040). When it moves a model from GPU to CPU, the quality, speed, sampling and prompt results were measured on the GPU, and nothing said so. Separately, a broken Vulkan binary was found only after a full round of failed answers.

A tune that does not probe the device starts the saved GPU backend first (`LlamaEngine.startBackend`, which shares the start-up code with a load) and stops with the reason when it cannot, before measuring or saving anything.
- **Consequences**: With the GPU broken, a quality-only run of the Coder stopped in 5 s with "vulkan could not be loaded" and the profile unchanged. content.text:
I made items 4, 5 and 7 and fixed the flaky test, and pushed them. Each was checked on this PC. The `tune:gate` baseline is the one item I haven't done, because it needs a working GPU (below).

**4. Context size now comes from free memory.** The tuner no longer "scores" context sizes on short questions, which all came out equal. It picks the largest of your listed sizes that fits comfortably (within 60%) in free VRAM on a GPU or free RAM on the CPU, no larger than the model was trained for. The KV cache is still measured at that size, and the profile records why: "8192 is the largest listed context that fits comfortably in 1.1 GiB free with a f16 KV cache". That's from a real run on SmolLM2, and yes, only about 1 GiB of RAM is free on this PC right now.

**5. Stages now record which device they were measured on.**
- **Profiles remember the CPU or GPU behind each stage.** If a Device re-run moves a model to another device, the stages measured on the old one get dotted chips and a warning. The row offers **Re-run Quality → Prompt**, which keeps the new device result and re-measures the rest on it.
- **Older profiles are covered too:** their device until now stands in for every stage.
- **A tune that starts on a saved GPU now checks the GPU first.** With your GPU in its current broken state, a quality-only run stopped after 5 seconds with "vulkan could not be loaded" and changed nothing.

**7. A real time estimate.** The made-up "≈ 9.3 h at 3 s per answer" is gone. The tune counts how many answers the chosen parts will ask and measures its own speed. The log and the model's row in the Bench section show "about 20 min left"; that's from a real tune started through the app. The figure is an upper bound, so tunes usually finish sooner.

**9. Loose ends**
- **Flaky test: fixed.** It didn't reproduce in 15 full test runs or 6 full gate runs. By reading the tests I found the likely cause: one check required a lock-file read to finish in 50 ms, which a busy Windows disk can miss. It now allows 1 second, which is still far below the real failure it guards against. That loosens a test, so ADR-043 records it.
- **`tune:gate` baseline: not done yet.** Creating it means fully re-tuning the three core models (several hours), and two of them run on the GPU, which is still broken. A baseline made now would quietly fall back to the CPU and lock in the wrong settings.

**Your next step:** restart the PC, which usually clears the GPU fault. Then tell me, and I'll start `npm run tune:gate -- --update-baseline` in the background and report when the baseline is in.
What else can be done?=

Here's what's left, best value first. I'm counting only what isn't built yet.

**Make the numbers trustworthy**
1. **Check each preset on held-back questions.** The preset is still chosen and scored on the same questions, so "+12.7 pts vs defaults" is optimistic. Hold back about a quarter of each task's questions and report the preset against the defaults only on those. A preset that doesn't beat the defaults there falls back to them.
2. **Tune "reasoning on" together with answer length.** "Think first" with a 512-token cap gets cut off and loses unfairly. Give it more room when it's tried (same idea for temperature with answer length).

**Make tuning faster**

3. **Drop clear losers early.** A sequential test could drop a clearly worse value after about 12 questions and spend the questions on close calls. That matters most for the 22 system prompts, the most expensive step.
4. **Start from a sibling model's results.** Qwen 0.5B Q4, Q5 and Q8 are the same model at different precisions: tune one, then only confirm and adjust the others. That's hours saved per model.
5. **Spot-check instead of re-tuning.** After a driver, runtime or test-suite change, re-measure each saved preset on about 12 questions and re-tune only what got worse. Right now every profile says "Re-tune ⚠" after any version change.

**New things the tuner could answer**

6. **Best model per task on this PC.** From the tuned profiles, show a small table: "for code, Qwen2.5 Coder 1.5B, 87.5%, on the GPU". Chat could suggest it when you pick the Code task.
7. **Which quantization to keep.** You have Q4, Q5 and Q8 of Qwen 0.5B. After tuning, the app could say whether the bigger files actually answer better on this PC, or just use more memory and disk.
8. **Per-task stage buttons.** Today the Sampling and Prompt buttons run all four tasks. Clicking just "Prompt · Code" would be much faster when only one task matters.

**Smaller fixes I noticed**

9. A model row shows only its *first* warning. With a suite change and a device change at once, the device warning is only visible in Details.
10. The old "Optimise one model" control is still in the benchmark section. It overlaps with the tuner now and could go.
11. The `tune:gate` baseline is still open, waiting for a working GPU (restart first).

**My suggestion:** 1 and 2 first, because they fix numbers that are currently wrong or optimistic. Then 6, the most useful new feature, then 4 and 5 to save time. Tell me which ones to do.

### ADR-046: Reasoning is tried with room to answer
- **Date**: 2026-10-31
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: The prompt stage tried reasoning off against deep (ADR-041) at the task's tuned answer length, often 512 tokens. A model told to think before answering can be cut off before it answers, so deep lost for lack of room rather than on merit.
- **Decision**: An axis may `widen` a value on top of the current settings and name the further settings it changes in `extraKeys`. The reasoning axis tries every value other than off with an answer length of at least `REASONING_TOKENS` (1024), or the task's own length if larger, and the stored preset keeps that length, so a winning deep is not cut off in use. Temperature and answer length are already re-tuned against each other by the descent's second pass.
- **Consequences**: Reasoning trials cost more tokens. A synthetic task that deep solves only with room now picks deep with 1024 tokens.
EOF

- **Date**: 2026-10-31
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: A model row showed only its first warning, so a device change behind a suite change was visible only in Details. The benchmark gate still offered "Optimise one model" (ADR-026), a 17-variant reload sweep on the smoke set that the settings tuner now does per stage, with statistics.
- **Decision**: The row shows each warning's first clause on its own line; "Measured before that" (which only explains the suite line) and "The tune's test items changed" (which always comes with a suite change) stay in Details. The "Optimise one model" selector and its code leave the panel; `npm run bench -- --model <id>` still runs the sweep from the command line, and saved single-model reports still display.
- **Consequences**: Rows can be two or three lines taller when several things changed. The panel has one way to tune a model.
EOF

All six items are done and pushed except the `tune:gate` baseline, which is now running in the background. That run is several hours: it fully re-tunes three models.

**2. Reasoning "on" gets room to answer.** When the tuner tries "think before answering", it now allows at least 1,024 tokens (more if the task already allows more). If thinking wins, the saved preset keeps that length, so it isn't cut off in real chats either. Temperature and answer length already get re-tuned against each other in the tuner's second round.

**6. Best model per task on this PC.** A new table under the model list shows, for each task, the best tuned model, its share of right answers with a 95% range, its device, and the runner-up. It compares only models tuned on the current test suite, because scores on different questions aren't comparable. Right now every profile is from an older suite, so it shows the older bests, marked "older test suite", until you re-tune.

**8. Per-task buttons.** In a model's **Details**, each task now has **Sampling** and **Prompt** buttons that run that stage for that task only. I checked one in the app: it sends exactly "prompt for code" and keeps everything else.

**9. Every warning on the row.** A model row now lists each reason it's out of date, including "Measured on the vulkan GPU, now on the CPU". Duplicate lines stay in Details.

**10. "Optimise one model" is gone** from the Bench section; the tuner does that job now. The command-line version (`npm run bench -- --model …`) still exists.

**11. `tune:gate` baseline.** It runs in a temporary folder, so your saved profiles aren't touched. It only writes `benchmarks/baseline-profiles.json`. I'll check the result and commit it when it finishes. Please keep heavy programs closed meanwhile: speed is part of what it measures.

**Corrections and slips:**
- **My Vulkan checks today were wrong, but the GPU fault was real.** I tested it with `node -e`, which breaks node-llama-cpp's self-test, so those checks could never pass. The earlier failures happened in real tunes, though, and your restart fixed it. Tested properly, Vulkan works and a real GPU tune runs ("16384 fits comfortably in 14.8 GiB free").
- **I rewrote four unpushed commits before pushing.** The secret scan flagged a harmless line (`maxTokens: Math.max(…)`), and the "this is fine" marker had to sit in the commit that added it. The push then needed the UI task re-recorded, because the rebase changed line endings on disk. The content is unchanged.
What else

Here's what's still open. The baseline run is still going in the background, and I'll report when it's done.

**From the earlier list, not built yet**
1. **Check each preset on held-back questions.** This is the most important one left. Presets are still chosen and scored on the same questions, so "+N pts vs defaults" is optimistic. Hold back about a quarter of each task's questions and report the honest gain on those. A preset that doesn't beat the defaults there falls back to them.
2. **Drop clear losers early.** Stop testing a clearly worse value after about 12 questions and spend the questions on close calls. This speeds up the system-prompt step most, the slowest part.
3. **Start from a sibling model.** Tune Qwen 0.5B Q4 once, then only confirm the result for Q5 and Q8. That's hours saved per model.
4. **Spot-check instead of re-tuning.** After a driver or version change, re-measure each preset on about 12 questions and re-tune only what got worse. Today every profile shows "Re-tune ⚠" after any change.
5. **Which quantization to keep.** For your three Qwen 0.5B files, say whether Q5 or Q8 actually answers better on this PC, or just costs memory and disk.

**Small follow-ups to today's work**

6. **Suggest the best model in chat.** When you pick the Code task and a better tuned model exists, say so next to the task picker. That's the second half of item 6, which I didn't build.
7. **Re-tune everything on the current suite.** Every profile is still from suite v8 and was measured before the system-prompt fix, so the "best model" table can't compare fairly yet. Once the baseline finishes, a **Run all** overnight would fix that. It doesn't need code, just the machine's time.

**My suggestion:** 1 next, since it's what makes every number in the app honest. Then 7 overnight, then 3 and 4 to cut future tuning time. Tell me which ones to do.

"Drop clear losers early. Stop testing a clearly worse value after about 12 questions and spend the questions on close calls. This speeds up the system-prompt step most, the slowest part." Maybe we can do this on prompt part only? %25 of Items, then continue with rest? What do you say?

Yes, I think that's a good design, and the prompt stage is the right place for it. It's the costliest part: 22 prompts × 48 questions per task, with nothing eliminated along the way. Two refinements, so it doesn't throw away a good prompt by bad luck:

**How I'd do it**
1. **Screening round:** every prompt answers the first 25% of the task's questions (12 of 48).
2. **Drop only clear losers.** At 12 questions one or two answers are noise, so "below average" isn't enough. A prompt is dropped when it's at least 3 questions behind the leader on those 12.
   - That's a real gap at 12 questions.
   - It also loses almost nothing: under the new "change only on a significant gain" rule, a challenger needs a strong win over the current prompt (p ≤ 0.2/21 on 48 questions). One that starts 3 behind essentially never gets there.
3. **The current prompt is never dropped,** since everything is measured against it.
4. **The survivors answer the remaining 36 questions,** and the final decision uses all 48, exactly as today.

**What it saves:** if about 6 of 22 prompts survive, each task needs about 480 answers instead of 1,056, roughly 55% less. At temperature > 0 (3 seeds) that's 3,168 answers down to about 1,440. It also stays consistent with the significance rule: the decision itself is unchanged; it just stops spending answers on prompts that couldn't win anyway.

**One thing to know:** reasoning and prompt repeat only have 2 values each, so screening doesn't help them. It's just for the system prompt.

I'd also show it in "What was tried": the dropped prompts listed with their 12-question score and "dropped after 12 questions".

Want me to build it? One timing note: the baseline is still running. Changing the code mid-run doesn't affect it (it already loaded the old code), but its prompt stage will use the old, full method.
Build it however we need a statistics section for every tune run. we will keep every data and it will provide us with nice detailed results

content.text:
I tested this directly, and **yes, it happens**. Feeding correct answers in different wording through the real checkers, many fail:

| Check (questions using it) | Correct answers that pass | Correct answers that fail |
|---|---|---|
| Exact match (46) | 2 of 6 | "**3546**", "The PIN is 3546.", "PIN: 3546", "3546" followed by an explanation |
| One of a list (23) | 2 of 4 | "The meeting is in room C7.", "**C7**" |
| Multiple choice (27) | 4 of 7 | "Answer: B", "The answer is B.", "Option B" |
| Number (58) | 3 of 5 | "Answer: 15" with a check line after it, "won 15 games, 8 more than the 7 they lost" |
| Code (104 test sets) | — | A reply with a usage example *before* the function: only the first code block is tested, so the function is never seen |

Two of these are outright wrong rather than strict:
- **"Answer: B" scores as "A".** The multiple-choice check takes the first letter of the reply.
- **The number check takes the last number written,** so a correct answer followed by a check calculation fails.

This matters beyond the scores. A checker that punishes wording bends the tune toward settings that make answers *short*, not *right*. That may be part of why the "follow the output format exactly" system prompt keeps winning.

**I don't know yet how often it happens with real models,** because the run records don't keep the answer text. I recommend:
1. **Store the answer text** in the run records, so every failure can be looked at and counted.
2. **Make the checkers read answers the way a person would,** without accepting wrong ones:
   - remove bold and quote marks;
   - understand "Answer: X" and "The answer is X";
   - for numbers, prefer the one after "Answer:";
   - for code, test the block that actually defines the function.

   No "contains anywhere" matching, so "Is it 3546 or 4596?" still fails.
3. **Separate the two kinds of failure:** "wrong answer" vs "couldn't read the format", shown apart in the statistics.

**Which categories need more questions:**

| Task | Questions | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Chat | 54 | **Most need.** 24 are public multiple-choice and 11 are short facts. Only 6 test actual chat skills (following instructions, formatting). I'd add about 30: follow a constraint, list format, length limit, tone, JSON output. |
| Long context | 51 | **Second.** 40 are generated "look up a value" items, and only 3 are different kinds of long-document task. I'd add multi-step questions over longer documents, and summaries checked by key facts. |
| Code | 112 | Fine. |
| Math | 51 | Fine. |

Separately, categories with only 2–4 questions (format, knowledge, context, instruction) give meaningless per-category percentages in reports. That's reporting noise, not a tuning problem.

Status: the Statistics section is written and its tests pass; it still needs its screenshot review and commit, which I'll finish first. The baseline is still running in the background. Should I then do the checker fixes (1–3), and add the chat and long-context questions?
Fix.

Before changing the checkers, one thing to sort out. The baseline run in the background records scores under the *current* checkers and question set. Once these fixes land, those scores won't be comparable, and the gate would flag the change itself as a regression. So that baseline would be invalid the moment it's written. ### ADR-051: A stopped run can be continued where it left off
- **Date**: 2026-10-31
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: A tune saves after every finished setting, and a part run's parts that were not reached stay pending, so a stopped run's remaining work is known. But choosing the same stages again starts a part run, which measures done parts again (ADR-040).
- **Decision**: `planTune(..., { continueRun })` resumes the saved progress and measures only what is not done in the chosen stages and tasks, even on a stale profile, and skips when nothing is left; chosen settings run again. The CLI takes `--continue`, the scheduler passes it to each tune, and `POST /api/tune/start` takes `continue: true`, which never starts a stale profile over, whatever `forceStale` says. A continued run is recorded as its own run with `continueRun` in its request.
- **Consequences**: A real SmolLM2 speed run stopped after three settings continued at threads, measured nothing it had finished, and marked the stage done.
EOF

### ADR-052: Checkers read an answer the way a person would
- **Date**: 2026-10-31

Scoring wording biases tuning toward terse prompts rather than right answers.
- **Decision**: Exact and one-of checks compare against the places a person would look (the whole reply, its first and last line, any "Answer:" line), each also without an "Answer is" lead-in, a short "Label:" or a short "The X is (in)" sentence start, after removing Markdown emphasis, code marks and list markers; never "contains anywhere", so "3546 or 4596" and "not 3546" still fail. A choice check reads "Answer/Option/Choice B", "the answer is (B)", or a leading "B", "(B)", "B)" or "B.", and treats "B or C" as no choice. A number check prefers the number after the last "Answer", else the last number. A code check tests the last fenced block that defines the entry function, else the first block. Choice and number checks mark replies with nothing readable as `unreadable`, apart from wrong answers. The suite version moves to 12 with the new questions of the same change.
- **Consequences**: The correct-form probe now passes 6/6 exact, 4/4 one-of, 7/7 choice and 4/5 number (the last gives no "Answer:" though asked to). Scores of earlier suites are not comparable.

Everything you asked for is built, tested and pushed to GitHub (343 tests pass).

**Fixed: answers that were right but scored wrong**
- **Correct replies in different wording now pass:**

  | Check | Before | Now |
  |---|---|---|
  | Exact answer | 2 of 6 | 6 of 6 |
  | One of a list | 2 of 4 | 4 of 4 |
  | Multiple choice | 4 of 7 | 7 of 7 |
  | Numbers | 3 of 5 | 4 of 5 |

- **Two real bugs are gone:** "Answer: B" was read as A, and a check line written after a number answer made it fail. The remaining number case gives no "Answer:" line even though the question asks for one, so it still fails.
- **Code is tested from the block that defines the function,** not from a usage example placed before it.
- **Wrong and hedged answers still fail,** for example "3546 or 4596" or "not 3546". Nothing is matched just because it appears somewhere in the reply.

**New: wrong vs "couldn't be read"**
- Every answer's text is now kept in the run records.

I built the held-back check (item 1), tested it and pushed it. 346 tests pass.

**What it does:**
- **A quarter of every kind of question is now kept out of tuning.** It's taken per category, so for example math holds back both GSM8K and its own questions. That's roughly 22 for chat, 31 for code, 13 for math and 16 for long context.
- **Each finished preset is checked on those questions.** Once a task's preset is chosen, it's measured against the default settings on the held-back questions only, as a paired comparison. That's the honest result, shown in a new **"On unseen questions"** column in each model's Details and in each run's detail, for example "83.9% vs 74.2% default (+9.7 pts, p=0.375)".
- **A preset that does worse there than the defaults isn't used.** The task falls back to the defaults, and the column says "worse, so the defaults apply". The tests cover both cases: a preset that only memorised its tuning questions falls back, and a genuinely better one is kept.

**One trade-off:**
- **Math now tunes on 38 questions instead of 48;** the other tasks still tune on 47–48. If you want math back at 48, I'd add about 13 more math questions.
- **I changed one existing test to match.** It required at least 48 tuning questions for every task; it now requires at least 36. ADR-054 records that.

**The baseline:**
- **It's running again, now on the final code** (suite v12, new answer checking, held-back questions). Your saved profiles aren't touched.
- **I stopped it once more first.** The held-back split changes which questions it measures on, so a baseline made before this change would have been invalid. It had only been running for a few minutes.
- **It will take many hours.** Please keep heavy programs closed while it runs.

**Before pushing,** the secret scan flagged one harmless line in the new code (a category label). As before, I folded the "this is fine" marker into the unpushed commit that added the line.

I stopped the three-model baseline run, nothing is left running from it, and its temporary folder is gone.

The baseline is now running on **one model, Qwen2.5 Coder 1.5B, in a single pass**. I picked the Coder because it's the model you chose for single runs before. To make this possible, `npm run tune:gate -- --update-baseline` has two new options:
- **`--models`** picks which of the three core models to tune. An unknown name is refused with the valid choices listed.
- **`--passes`** limits the tuner's rounds.

The regular gate check then tests whatever models the baseline contains. All 346 tests pass and the change is committed; I'll push it with the baseline file.

improve the tuner ui. also running tunes should update in realtime. add sections under that place.

I'll take "sections under that place" to mean a **live panel under the tuner's controls** that fills in while a tune runs. Here's the plan:

**Real time instead of polling every 2 seconds**
- The server pushes each change to the browser over a live connection (server-sent events) as it happens.
- If that connection drops, the app falls back to polling.

**The live panel's sections**

| Section | Shows |
|---|---|
| **Now running** | Each running model, its lane (CPU/GPU), stage and setting, a progress bar (answers measured against expected) and the time left |
| **Trying now** | The values of the current setting, each with its score and response time, updated as each result arrives |
| **Decided this run** | Every finished setting: what it chose, whether it changed or was kept, and why |
| **Queue** | Models waiting, finished, skipped or failed, with the reason for failures |

**Tidier structure:** the tuner area gets clear headings: Run a tune → Live → Models → Best model per task → Continue → Tune runs and statistics → Tune settings.

The baseline is still running on the GPU in the background, so I'll build and unit-test now. The visual check with a real tune waits until the baseline finishes, because a second tune would distort its speed measurements.

### ADR-055: A running tune is shown live
- **Date**: 2026-11-01
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: The Bench panel polled the tune status every two seconds and showed only each model's last event (stage, setting, time left); which values were being tried, how they scored and what was decided were visible only after the run.
- **Decision**: The scheduler keeps a live summary per model from the tune's events: answers so far against the expected count, the latest time left, the setting being tried with each value's latest round (score, time, tokens), and the last 30 decisions with their reasons. It calls subscribers after every change. `GET /api/tune/stream` sends the job at once and then after each change as server-sent events, gathering changes within 250 ms and sending a keep-alive comment every 15 s, and stops listening when the page goes away. The panel listens to it while open and falls back to polling if the stream fails.
- **Consequences**: The panel shows a running tune's sections as it goes. A tune started outside the app (the CLI, the tune gate) is not part of the scheduler and is not shown live.

Running tunes now update in real time, with the new sections under the tuner's controls. All 349 tests pass and it's pushed to GitHub.

**What you'll see while a tune runs.** A highlighted **Running now** panel appears below the Run all / Cancel buttons:

| Section | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **One card per running model** | Its lane (CPU/GPU), stage and setting (e.g. "Prompt for Code: System prompt"), a progress bar of answers measured against expected, and the time left |
| **Trying now** | Each value of the current setting with how many questions it has answered, its score, time and tokens. The current best is highlighted: highest score, or for speed settings the fastest time. |
| **Decided this run** | The latest decisions and why, e.g. "Context size: 16384 — the largest that fits in 14.8 GiB free" or "Kept 0.2: … short of the p ≤ 0.04 a change needs" |
| **Queue** | Waiting, finished and failed models, with the reason for any failure |

A **Models** heading now separates the panel from the model list.

**Real time:**
- **The server pushes each change the moment it happens,** bundled to at most 4 updates a second, instead of the app asking every 2 seconds.
- **The connection closes** when you close the dialog.
- **A fallback covers browsers the stream can't serve:** a browser on another computer has to send the access key, which a stream connection can't carry, so it falls back to polling every 2 seconds.

**How it's checked so far:**
- **Unit tests** cover the scheduler's live summary and the server stream: the job is sent at once, then each change, and listening stops when the page closes.
- **The panel's layout** I checked in the browser with a *simulated* stream: two running models, one waiting, one finished.
- **The real end-to-end check is still to do.** A real tune through the app would distort the baseline, which is measuring speed right now. I'll do it as soon as the baseline finishes, and keep the task open until then.

**Limit:** only tunes started from the app appear live. A tune started from the command line, like the baseline running now, isn't part of the app, so it doesn't show there.

**The baseline (Coder only, one pass)** has been running since 22:08 and is still in progress. When it finishes, I'll do the real live check, commit the baseline file and push.

Here's the answer to your question first, then tabs.

**Does each best result apply to the other parts of tuning?** Partly, by design:

| Stage | Shared or per task | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Device (CPU/GPU) | Shared | Chosen once per model; every later stage runs on it. |
| Quality (context size, KV cache) | Shared | Chosen once per model, measured on a *mix* of all four tasks' questions. |
| Speed (threads, batch…) | Shared | Chosen once per model, on top of the above. |
| Sampling and prompt | **Per task** | Chat, code, math and long context each get their own, built on the shared settings above. |

The shared part is why one preset serves all chats without reloading the model. The cost is that the KV-cache choice is a compromise across tasks. If, say, a lighter cache hurt long context but not code, the mixed measurement could pick it anyway.

**On separating the testing more, which is ModelDuck's differentiator:** I'd **not** split the *presets* further, because fewer questions per preset makes the statistics weak again. I'd make the tests more *visible and separable*:

1. **Show results per question type inside each task.** For example, Code becomes "write a function / fix a bug / work in a codebase", and Chat becomes "follow a format / facts / truthfulness". A setting that helps one type and hurts another would then be visible, including on the held-back questions.
2. **Let quality settings be judged per task.** Measure the KV cache per task and keep the shared choice only if no task gets significantly worse; otherwise warn, and say which task loses.
3. **A "Benchmark" tab** describing the test suite itself: each task, its question types, how many questions, how they're checked, and how many are held back. That makes the differentiator visible in the app, not just the README.

Tell me which of 1–3 you want. Meanwhile I'll build the tabs.

- **Tune:** what to run, the live panel and Continue.
- **Models:** the model table and the best model per task.
- **Runs:** tune runs and statistics.
- **Settings:** the values each setting is tried at.
- **Benchmark gate:** the old reports.

- **Decision**: `benchmarks/own-items-v12.mjs` adds 30 chat items (instruction and format: bullets, JSON, YAML, a Markdown table, word limits, lowercase, no digits, no letter e, a start or end word, translation, tense, ordering, a polite refusal, a summary) with three new check types (`bulletCount`, `maxWords`, `containsAll`), and 12 long-context items generated from fixed seeds (two-step manager-to-room lookups, which delivery came first in a shuffled dated log, whether a parcel is listed, a budget code defined at the top and asked about a person far below). Every chat item has a reference reply that passes and a plausible wrong one that fails, and every long-context answer is read back from its own document, in `tests/benchmark-suite-v12.test.js`. With the answer readers of ADR-052 this is suite v12.
- **Consequences**: 310 items; chat 84, long context 63. Saved profiles show a suite-changed warning until re-tuned, and the tune:gate baseline must be made on v12.

### ADR-054: Each preset is checked on items it was never tuned on
- **Date**: 2026-10-31
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: A task's preset was chosen on its rungs and its gain over the defaults was measured on the same items, so the reported gain was optimistic (the best of many tries fits its own items), and a preset that only fitted those items was applied anyway.
- **Decision**: `taskHoldout` holds back the last quarter (rounded) of every category/dataset bucket of a task, so every kind of item is checked unseen; rungs come only from the rest. Once a task's sampling and prompt stages are both done (and when either changed), the tune scores the final preset and the untuned settings on the held-back items, paired, and records `holdout` (items, rate, range, default rate, paired change and p). A preset worse than the defaults there falls back: the task's stored settings become empty, so the defaults apply, and the record says so. The time-left estimate counts these answers. The rung test of ADR-038 now asks for at least 36 tuning items rather than 48, since math tunes on 38 of its 51; chat and code still tune on 48.
- **Consequences**: About 22, 31, 13 and 16 items are held back for chat, code, math and long context. The task hash changes, so saved profiles are stale until re-tuned, and the tune:gate baseline is made after this change.

### ADR-055: A running tune is shown live
- **Date**: 2026-11-01
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: The Bench panel polled the tune status every two seconds and showed only each model's last event (stage, setting, time left); which values were being tried, how they scored and what was decided were visible only after the run.
- **Decision**: The scheduler keeps a live summary per model from the tune's events: answers so far against the expected count, the latest time left, the setting being tried with each value's latest round (score, time, tokens), and the last 30 decisions with their reasons. It calls subscribers after every change. `GET /api/tune/stream` sends the job at once and then after each change as server-sent events, gathering changes within 250 ms and sending a keep-alive comment every 15 s, and stops listening when the page goes away. The panel listens to it while open and falls back to polling if the stream fails.
- **Consequences**: The panel shows a running tune's sections as it goes. A tune started outside the app (the CLI, the tune gate) is not part of the scheduler and is not shown live.

### ADR-056: Each task's result is broken down by question type
- **Date**: 2026-11-01
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: A task's preset was reported as one rate, so a setting that helped one kind of question (say, writing functions) and hurt another (fixing bugs) looked like a small net change. The benchmark is what sets ModelDuck apart, and its question types were invisible in the tuner.
- **Decision**: The tune takes `typeOf(itemId)` (the tune job passes each suite item's category), and a task's statistics and its held-back check carry `byType`: per question type, the items and right answers for the chosen settings and for the defaults. Details and a run's detail show them under "By question type" in plain words (for example "Work in a codebase", "GSM8K word problems"), with the types the preset answers worse than the defaults marked.
- **Consequences**: Per-type counts are small (often under 15), so they show where to look rather than prove a difference; the task-level paired test stays the decision rule.

### ADR-057: The shared quality settings are checked on every task
- **Date**: 2026-11-01
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: Device, quality and speed settings are shared by all of a model's tasks; only sampling and prompt are per task. The quality stage (context and KV cache) chooses on a mix of every task's items, so a setting much better on one task could win while clearly hurting another.
- **Decision**: After the quality stage, each task's share of the last load level (`rungs.loadByTask`) is scored with the chosen settings and with the settings before the stage, paired, from the answers the sweep already measured. A task worse at `changeAlpha` (0.2, uncorrected, so every task is protected) sends the quality settings back to those before the stage. The profile's load carries `perTask` (each task's rate before and after, p, worse) and `reverted` (the task that lost); Details and a run's detail state it.
- **Consequences**: A shared setting can no longer trade one task for another unnoticed. Since the check uses already-measured answers, it costs nothing extra.

content.text:
I've built all three proposals, and they're pushed (`64a6304..c8eaa77`). All 353 tests pass and the strict gate passed 4/4.

1. **Results by question type.** Each task's result is now split by question type, for example "Work in a codebase", "Fix a bug" and "GSM8K word problems". It shows the preset next to the defaults, both on the questions it was tuned on and on held-back questions. A type where the preset does worse than the defaults is marked. You'll find it in a model's Details and in each run's detail. Most types have fewer than 15 questions, so these numbers show where to look rather than prove a difference.
2. **Shared settings checked on every task.** Context size and KV cache are shared by all of a model's tasks. After choosing them, the tuner now checks each task on its own. If any task gets clearly worse, it goes back to the settings it had before. Details shows each task's result and which task caused the switch back. This reuses answers already measured, so it costs no extra time.
3. **New Benchmark tab** in the Tune & benchmark dialog. It describes the whole suite: version 12, 310 questions across Chat (84), Code (112), Math (51) and Long context (63). For each question type it shows how many questions there are, how many are held back, where they come from (ModelDuck's own, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MMLU or TruthfulQA) and how answers are checked, such as "code that passes its tests" or "chosen letter". It's built from the same questions and split the tuner uses, so it can't drift out of date. I checked it in headless Edge: no console errors, and the dialog reopens on the tab you last had open.

The one-model baseline for `qwen2.5-coder-1.5b-instruct-q4` is still running and has reached the Code sampling stage. It started before the first two changes, so its saved profile won't include the per-type and per-task numbers. That doesn't affect the gate. When it finishes, I'll check its results, then commit and push `benchmarks/baseline-profiles.json`.
So what else do you propose?

Here's what I'd do next, most useful first.

**For quality and your coding goal**
1. **Add questions to the thin types.** The Benchmark tab makes the gaps plain: Knowledge has 3 questions, and Fix several bugs, Fix a bug in a codebase and Write a long function have 6 each. Math tunes on 38 questions, not 48. With so few, the per-type results can only hint at a difference. I'd bring each type to at least 12, starting with the codebase ones.
2. **Harder codebase tests.** Today's codebase questions are one prompt, one answer. For "a coder that handles complex codebases", I'd add questions spread over several files, a fix that starts from a stack trace or failing test output, and an edit to an existing file that is checked by running its tests. This tests what you actually want the model to do.
3. **Show "too few to tell" on per-type rows.** Mark a type whose difference is within noise, so a red row on 4 questions isn't read as a real loss.

**For tune time**
4. **Re-check instead of re-tune.** When the runtime, driver or suite changes, first re-score the saved preset on the held-back questions (a few minutes). Only run a full re-tune if it got worse.
5. **Start from a sibling model's result.** A new quant of an already-tuned model would start from that model's preset, which should cut most of the tuning rounds.

**For users of the app**
6. **Suggest a model per task in chat.** For example: "for code, Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B scored best". The best-model table already holds this; the chat task picker just doesn't use it.
7. **Quantization advice.** Compare q4 and q8 of the same model per question type, and say whether the bigger file is worth the memory.

**Still open from before:** once the baseline finishes, I'll run a real tune through the app to confirm the live view works end to end.

I'd start with 1 and 2, because they make every other result more trustworthy and match your coding goal. Should I go ahead with those?

### ADR-059: Per-type results say when they are too few to tell
- **Date**: 2026-11-01
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: ADR-056 shows right answers per question type, but most types have under 15 items, so a row where the preset is two answers behind the defaults was marked as worse even when that is within noise.

- **AI benchmark gate** - two phases: model reload/quantization/KV-cache settings,
  then sampling/prompting settings, with test hashes so result changes are not

## AI benchmark gate

The required gate is `npm run tune:gate` (ADR-027). This seeded, batch-1
cross-model benchmark on the real `LlamaEngine` is optional: the **model reload**
phase (`npm run bench`) changes one load setting at a time across models, and the
**model usage** phase (`npm run bench:chat`) compares sampling and prompting on a
chosen configuration.

Three small model classes are the default required set: SmolLM2 135M (tiny), Qwen2.5
0.5B (general) and Qwen2.5 Coder 1.5B (code). `--full-matrix` / `npm run bench:full`
adds Qwen2.5 1.5B, Llama 3.2 3B and Phi-3.5 Mini plus their KV-cache variants; that
deeper review takes hours on a CPU and is opt-in. Suite v13 runs 344 items: 284
questions ModelDuck authored (code, multi-file codebases, bug fixes, chat, math,
long context, comprehension, facts) plus 60 items copied from
permissively licensed public benchmarks (GSM8K 16, MMLU 12,
HumanEval 12, MBPP 8 and TruthfulQA 12) with source and licence recorded per item;
see [benchmarks/NOTICE-benchmarks.md](benchmarks/NOTICE-benchmarks.md). Public items
may be in a model's training data, so the report shows **own questions** and
**public benchmarks** as separate origins, with public results per dataset.

```bash
npm run bench -- --download        # first run: fetch missing models, core phase
npm run bench:all                  # optional: add the model-usage phase
npm run bench:full                 # optional: add Llama 3B and Phi 3.8B
npm run bench -- --model <id>      # settings sweep for one model; never touches a baseline
npm run bench:update               # deliberately replace both baselines
npm run bench:update:model         # deliberately replace only the model baseline
npm run bench:update:full          # replace the model baseline with six models
npm run bench:report
npm run bench:link                 # after commit: attach the run to HEAD
npm run verify:manifest -- --models-dir ..\models
```

`verify:manifest` is an opt-in real-model check that does not write history or
change baselines. It proves session reuse, 40-message truncation, prompt
repetition, a completion after a chat session, chat-template identity and runtime
identity on an installed GGUF.

I've built all three, and they're pushed (`c8eaa77..22d4dab`). All 362 tests pass and the strict gate passed 4/4.

1. **"Too few to tell" on per-type rows.** Each question type now gets its own statistical test comparing the preset with the defaults on the same questions. The "By question type" table has a new Difference column showing "clearly better", "clearly worse", "too few to tell" or "same". Only clearly worse rows are marked red. Profiles tuned before this show "–" there. I checked it in headless Edge with sample data.
2. **Thin types filled (suite v13).** I added 9 knowledge questions, 6 long functions to write, 6 long functions with several bugs, and 13 math word problems.
   - Knowledge, long functions and long bug fixes now have 12 questions each.
   - Math has 64, so it now tunes on 48 questions like chat and code (it was 38).
   - Tests confirm every reference answer passes, every buggy version fails, and every math answer matches an independent calculation.
3. **Harder codebase tests.** There's a new 7-file task-planner codebase, plus 12 items on it and on the existing ones:
   - **6 changes that touch more than one function or file**, for example task priorities, a transfer fee, stacked discount codes and numbered lists in the Markdown renderer.
   - **6 fixes that start from a failing test and its output**, as you'd paste it, where the cause is in a different file from where it fails. For example, a "no account for Ann" error is raised in `getAccount`, but the cause is in `openAccount`.
   - The answer may change any functions and use several code blocks. A hidden check runs the result afterwards. Tests confirm each quoted test output is what the broken code really produces.

To make room for the new questions in the README I trimmed three sentences: the default model list, the full benchmark run's description and the `verify:manifest` description.

**Decision for you:** I stopped the one-model baseline that was running. Adding questions makes every saved profile and the tune:gate baseline out of date, so the old run's result would have been useless. A new baseline needs a re-tune on v13, which takes a few hours for the Coder model alone. Should I start it now?
no, what else do you propose for tuning

Here's what I'd change in the tuner, most useful first.

**Save time**
1. **Reuse answers across runs.** Each run already caches answers within itself. Keeping them across runs would mean a re-tune only answers questions it hasn't seen before. An answer is only reused when the model file, runtime, settings, seed and question are all the same. This matters right now: v13 made every profile stale, but 310 of its 356 questions are unchanged. A re-tune would mostly ask the 46 new ones, so minutes instead of hours.
2. **Re-check before re-tuning.** When the suite or runtime changes, first score the saved preset on the held-back questions. Only re-tune the parts that got worse.
3. **Stop a round once it's decided.** If a candidate is so far behind that it couldn't catch up even by winning every remaining question, drop it right away. The result can't change, so this is pure saving.
4. **Start from a sibling model's result.** A new quant of an already-tuned model would start from that model's settings, so most tuning rounds end quickly.

**Get better results**
5. **Split a task when its question types disagree.** If a setting is clearly better for one type and clearly worse for another, for example writing functions versus fixing bugs, tune separate presets for each. Until now these differences couldn't be told apart; the new "clearly better / clearly worse" check makes them visible.
6. **Check pairs of settings together.** The tuner changes one setting at a time, so it misses pairs that only help in combination, such as temperature with top-p. After the normal pass, a small check would try the best two values of the two settings that mattered most, together.
7. **Measure speed on long prompts too.** Speed is measured mostly on short questions. Long-context and codebase use depend on how fast the prompt is read, so the chosen settings could be slow exactly where it matters.

I'd start with 1 and 2. Together they turn the v13 re-tune you just declined, and every future suite change, from hours into minutes. Want me to build those?
I'll start by reading the parts of the tuner these four touch: the round loop, the per-task stages and the speed stage.
